newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BOE data shows Britain still borrowing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BOE data shows Britain still borrowing.

text.p: British consumers continued to borrow heavily in October to finance strong high street spending, Bank of England figures showed on Friday, suggesting retailers are in for bumper pre-Christmas sales.
Britain's Central Bank data showed net consumer credit dipped to 856 million pounds ($1.44 billion) in October from 1.041 billion in September.

Economists said despite the decline, the figures were still robust, although a return to the debt-financed boom of the 1980s was unlikely, with a debt overhang from the recession keeping a lid on consumers' ability to borrow more.
"Consumers haven't really paid off any debt since the trough of the recession...so there's not the same scope to take on more in the coming year," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.
"That's one crucial reason why we're not heading for a repeat of the 1980s boom."
The figures provide further evidence that demand is strong in the British economy and that interest rates might have to rise further to prevent a resurgence in inflation.
Philip Uglow, economist at Union Discount, said Friday's consumer credit data certainly did nothing to dent the argument for another interest rate rise.

"The figures were weaker than we expected, but I don't think they add anything new to the interest rate debate," he said. "Recent credit figures, and even this morning's, show that consumer demand is bubbling along at quite a healthy pace."
In recent months consumers have steadily returned to the high street, with economists predicting this trend will continue over the next year or so.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said in his budget speech on Tuesday that consumer spending would grow by 4.25 percent in 1997.

He nevertheless predicted that underlying inflation would remain under control, dipping to 2.5 percent in 1997 after surging unexpectedly to 3.3 percent in October -- a forecast greeted with some scepticism by economists.

Two of the Chancellor's independent economic advisers told a House of Commons Treasury select committee on Thursday that interest rates would have to rise to dampen growing consumer demand and prevent a resurgence of inflation.
"Demand is now growing too rapidly," said Goldman Sachs' chief economist and "wise man" Gavyn Davies. "The implication is that interest rates have to go up further."
Clarke raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point at the end of October to 6.0 percent. He now faces the dilemma of whether to raise rates again before the general election.
If he does, he risks alienating an already critical British electorate. If he does not, inflation could get out of control.
The government must hold a general election by May 22. The ruling Conservatives trail their Labour Party rivals by up to 20 points in the polls and face an uphill struggle to get re-elected.
